entries.content: S* = GFP - V* (equivalently S* = TP* - C*_m - V*). Surplus value is the portion of new value created in production that is not paid to productive workers. It is the source of profit, rent, interest, taxes, and unproductive wages in the Marxian framework.
Derived from S503 (GFP) minus S504 (V*). Book period from Table 5.5. Extension spliced at 1989: for the extended period, S* = GFP_extended - V*_extended, though GFP extension is constrained by S502.
Fig 5.4 shows S* as the surplus component of GFP in the full revenue account. Fig 9.1 uses S* in long-run accumulation analysis showing that surplus value growth drives capital accumulation.

Surplus value in the Marxian sense is fundamentally different from profit in orthodox accounts. S* includes not just corporate profits but also the portions of rent, interest, indirect taxes, and unproductive-sector wages that originate as transfers from the surplus created in production.

Mohun (2013) finds surplus value growing relative to V* over 1964-2010, consistent with ST's findings for 1948-1989. Mohun's exploitation rates are ~2.3-2.5 vs ST's 2.6-2.7, reflecting the broader productive sector classification. See mohun_exploitation_rates*.csv.

S* extension beyond 1989 is doubly constrained: by S502 (for GFP) and by S504 extension quality. If GFP is approximated via BEA value-added for productive sectors, the resulting S* carries both approximation errors.

[internal-decision-record]: DIV-001 (K→K* capital stock restriction) is BLOCKED pending a comprehensive unit audit. S505 (S*) is in millions from Table 5.7, while K from BEA Fixed Assets uses a different unit convention (UNIT_MULT=6). Computing S*/K or any ratio involving both series produces inflated results until unit normalization is completed. The S*/K ratio for profit rate purposes must not be computed until the unit mismatch is resolved. ADJ-001 remains BLOCKED.

The estimates of variable capital in the previous section allow us to calculate surplus value and surplus product. By definition, S* = VA* − V* = surplus value (in money form); S*/V* = rate of surplus value; NP* = the necessary product (consumption of productive workers) = V*; SP* = FP* − NP* = surplus product.
entries.context: Section 5.4 (pp. 113-114) — canonical definition of S* as Marxian value-added minus variable capital. This is the identity S505 implements as S503 (GFP/VA*) − S504 (V*).

entries.content: P+ is intended as a 'naive' measure of surplus value, as directly derived from NIPA. Since NIPA does not estimate the wage equivalent, the only wage cost directly shown would be EC. Hence, P+ = VA−EC = NNP−EC.
entries.context: Footnote 14, p. 114 — distinguishes S* from the orthodox 'naive' surplus measure P+. Anchors the divergence between S505 and any profit-type aggregate computed from NIPA EC alone; warrants S505 ≠ corporate profits.

entries.content: For U.S. data, the orthodox measure VA = P + EC remains within 10% of the Marxian measure VA* = V* + S*, so the difference between P/EC and S*/V* is largely due to the fact that V* = Wp << EC. But we cannot assume that the rough equality that holds for the United States between the two value-added measures is a universal phenomenon.
entries.context: Footnote 15, p. 114 — quantifies the VA* vs VA gap (≤10% for U.S.) and locates the principal source of S*/V* >> P/EC in the V* << EC inequality. Bounds the magnitude of error from approximating S* via NIPA value-added in the extension period.

entries.content: Figure 5.12 compares real surplus value and real profits (defined here as real P). Both rise strongly, but not equally so; real surplus value rises about 16% relative to real profits.
entries.context: Section 5.4, Figure 5.12 (p. 114) — empirical magnitude: real S* grows ~16% more than real profits 1948-1989. Documents the level/trend divergence between S505 and orthodox profit aggregates.
